# Reading a gene

Here is a real line from a real clinical database. A deletion of two bases in
*BRCA1*, classified as pathogenic by an expert panel, sits at position
43,124,028 on chromosome 17. Here is the same deletion, in the same gene, from
the same database: position 41,276,045 on chromosome 17.

Both are correct. They differ by 1,847,983 bases, which is about fifteen times
the length of the entire gene. Nothing on either page is wrong, and nothing on
either page will stop you writing down the wrong one. By the end of this
chapter you'll know what the second number is, why it's still in circulation,
and how to tell which one a paper means.

## What is actually in a database record

When people say they looked a gene up in NCBI, they usually mean one of three
different records, and the three answer different questions.

The **Gene** record is about the gene as a piece of the genome. Where it sits,
what it's called, what it's been called before, which papers mention it. The
**Nucleotide** record is about a sequence: a specific string of A, C, G and T
that somebody deposited, with a specific length. The **Protein** record is
about what that sequence codes for.

One gene therefore has one Gene record and many Nucleotide records, because a
gene can be transcribed into several different [transcripts]{.term def="One RNA
version of a gene, differing from the others in which exons it includes."} and
each one is its own sequence. Get that straight first,
because a lot of confusing answers come from comparing a number off one record
with a number off another.

### Sequences travel as FASTA

Every sequence you download from anywhere arrives in a format that has barely
changed since 1985. This is [FASTA]{.term def="A plain-text sequence format. A header line starting
with a greater-than sign, then the sequence."}, and it looks like this:

``` {.default filename="data/sequences/brca1_five_species.fasta"}
>human|NM_007294.4 Homo sapiens BRCA1 mRNA
GCTGAGACTTCCTGGACCCCGCACCAGGCTGTGGGGTTTCTCAGATAACTGGGCCCCTGC
GCTCAGGAGGCCTTCACCCTCTGCTCTGGGTAAAGTTCATTGGAACAGAAAGAAATGGAT
```

The rules are short. A line starting with `>` is a header and everything after
the `>` is a description of whatever follows. Every line until the next `>` is
sequence. Nothing else is required.

What the format does not do is tell you anything about the sequence. It won't
say which organism it came from, or which build of the genome it matches, or
whether it's DNA or RNA or protein. All of that lives in the header, and the
header is free text. Different tools put different things there in different
orders, and some put nothing at all.

::: {.trap}
Most software treats everything up to the first space as the sequence's
identifier and throws the rest away. So `>human|NM_007294.4 Homo sapiens BRCA1
mRNA` becomes `human|NM_007294.4`, and the species silently disappears. If two
of your sequences have headers that agree up to the first space, they'll end up
with the same identifier and one of them will overwrite the other. You'll meet
this for real in Chapter 15.
:::

### The accession number and the part after the dot

The human *BRCA1* transcript in that file is `NM_007294.4`. That's an
[accession number]{.term def="A permanent identifier for one database record.
The part after the dot rises each time the sequence is corrected."}, and it's
the single most useful thing on the page.

Read it in three pieces.

The prefix `NM_` tells you where the record came from. `NM_` means a
curated messenger RNA: a human being at NCBI has looked at this and signed off
on it. You'll also see `XM_`, which means the same kind of thing produced
automatically by software from a genome annotation, with nobody checking. Both
are useful. Only one of them is evidence that the transcript was ever observed.

`007294` is the record. It will never be reused and never point at a different
gene.

`.4` is the edition. It means this sequence has been corrected three times
since it was first deposited. When somebody fixes a base, the number after the
dot goes up and the old version stays available forever.

That last part is what makes a result reproducible. `NM_007294` means whatever
is current today. `NM_007294.4` means exactly 7,088 specific bases in a
specific order, and it will still mean those bases in ten years. Write down the
version. Every time.

### Which transcript, when there are several

*BRCA1* has more than one transcript, so "the *BRCA1* sequence" isn't a
well-formed request. For most of the last twenty years the honest answer to
"which one should I use" was that it depended, and that answer is useless to
somebody who has to pick one and move on.

Since 2018 there's been a better one. NCBI and EMBL-EBI went through the human
genes one at a time and agreed on a single representative transcript for each,
matching perfectly between their two databases. That agreed transcript is the
[MANE Select]{.term def="The one transcript per human gene that NCBI and
EMBL-EBI agree is representative."} transcript, and it's flagged on the record.

So: when you need one human transcript and have no specific reason to want
another, use the MANE Select one. This book will use it throughout, and you can
too, without having to justify the choice every time.

MANE covers human. It does not cover mouse, which is why Exercise 5.2 will feel
different.

## Walkthrough: looking up BRCA1

Open `ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene` and search for `BRCA1 human`. The record you want
is Gene ID 672.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live NCBI interface on 2 August 2026. NCBI redesigns these
pages every few years and the labels move. Three things are always on the Gene
record under some name: where the gene is, what it's called, and a list of its
transcripts. Find those and the layout doesn't matter.
:::

Here's what that record says, and what each part means.

**It's on chromosome 17, at 17q21.31.** The `17q21.31` is a cytogenetic band,
which is a coordinate system based on the stripes you can see down a stained
chromosome under a microscope. It's coarse, it predates sequencing, and you
will still see it in papers.

**It spans 126,033 bases of `NC_000017.11`.** That accession is chromosome 17
itself. The gene runs from 43,170,326 down to 43,044,294, and the fact that the
start is bigger than the stop is not a typo. It means the gene is read off the
other strand, right to left as the coordinates are printed. About a third of
human genes are.

**Its MANE Select transcript is `NM_007294.4`, which is 7,088 bases.**

Stop on those two numbers for a second. The gene occupies 126,033 bases of
chromosome. The transcript is 7,088 bases. The difference is introns, which get
cut out, and it means that if you mix up "the gene" and "the transcript" you
are wrong by a factor of about eighteen.

**Its protein is `NP_009225.1`, which is 1,863 amino acids.**

You can check that number without trusting anybody. The record says the coding
sequence runs from base 114 to base 5,705 of the transcript. Subtract, and add
one because the range includes both ends: 5,705 − 114 + 1 = 5,592 bases. Three
bases per amino acid gives 1,864 codons, and one of those is the stop codon,
which isn't an amino acid. 1,863. It matches.

<!-- nlr-allow: 1864 5591 -->

::: {.check}
Do that subtraction yourself before reading on. If you got 5,591, you forgot
that the range includes both ends. That off-by-one is the single most common
bug in this entire field, it has an entire section of Chapter 11 to itself, and
it starts here.
:::

### The chapter's real lesson: three exon counts, none of them wrong

Somewhere on that same page you'll find that *BRCA1* has 22 exons. Somewhere
else on the same page, you'll find 31. The transcript record lists 23.

None of these is a mistake, and nobody is going to flag the disagreement for
you.

- **22** comes from the prose summary at the top of the record, which is
  written by hand and describes the gene as the literature has traditionally
  counted it.
- **31** counts every exon that appears in *any* annotated transcript of the
  gene. Different transcripts use different exons, and this number is the union
  of all of them.
- **23** is the number of exons in `NM_007294.4` specifically, which is the one
  transcript you actually chose.

They're three answers to three different questions: what does the literature
say, what does this gene do in total, and what's in the sequence in front of
me. The number you want is almost always the third one, because it's the only
one attached to a specific sequence you can point at.

::: {.why}
This is the habit the rest of the book is built on. Before you write a number
down, ask what question it answers. A number in biology is almost never a
property of the organism. It's a property of a measurement, or of a database
record, or of a decision somebody made about which transcript to call the real
one. Chapter 7 does this again with E-values, Chapter 20 does it with read
counts, and Chapter 25 does it with p-values.
:::

### Back to the two coordinates

The variant from the opening is written `NM_007294.4(BRCA1):c.68_69del`. Now
you can read it. It's a deletion of the two bases at positions 68 and 69 of the
coding sequence of that exact transcript version, and because it removes two
bases rather than three it shifts the reading frame and destroys everything
downstream.

That description doesn't mention a chromosome at all, which is why it survives
intact while the chromosomal coordinates move.

They move because the coordinates are counted from the start of a
[genome assembly]{.term def="One numbered reconstruction of a genome. A
coordinate only means something relative to a named assembly."}, and there's
more than one assembly. GRCh37 came out in 2009,
GRCh38 in 2013. Between them, sequence was added, removed and reordered, so
every coordinate downstream of any change shifted. The same variant is at
41,276,045 in GRCh37 and 43,124,028 in GRCh38.

::: {.trap}
A coordinate with no assembly attached is not a location. If you take
41,276,045 from a 2012 paper and look it up in a current genome browser,
you'll land 1.8 megabases away from *BRCA1*, in the middle of a different gene,
and the browser will show you a perfectly ordinary page. Nothing errors.
:::

So when a paper gives you a coordinate, find the assembly before you use it.
It's usually in the methods section, and if it isn't, that tells you something
about the paper.

## Exercises

::: {.exercise num="5.1" time="25 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Retrieve the human *BRCA1* record and write down what the database actually
says, rather than what you remember it saying.
:::
::: {.produce}
Five values: the chromosome, the genomic span in bases, the accession of the
MANE Select transcript including its version suffix, that transcript's length
in bases, and the length of the protein in amino acids.
:::
::: {.check}
Your span should be a six-figure number and your transcript length a
four-figure one. If they're the same order of magnitude, you've recorded the
same thing twice. Then check the protein: subtract the two ends of the coding
range, add one, divide by three, subtract one for the stop codon. It should
land exactly on the number the protein record gives.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="6"}
:::
:::

::: {.exercise num="5.2" time="25 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Find the same gene in mouse, and record what changed.
:::
::: {.given}
The mouse gene is called `Brca1`. Mouse gene symbols are written with one
capital and the rest lowercase, where human ones are all capitals. That
convention is real, it's enforced by two different nomenclature committees, and
it will break a string comparison in Chapter 20 if you forget it.
:::
::: {.produce}
The same five values as Exercise 5.1, plus one sentence naming the largest
proportional difference between the two species and saying whether it surprises
you.
:::
::: {.check}
The mouse gene occupies roughly half the chromosome that the human one does,
but its protein is only about 3 percent shorter. Those two facts are not in
tension, and being able to say why is the point of the exercise. One more
thing: look for the MANE Select flag on the mouse record. It isn't there. Write
down why not.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="7"}
:::
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="Your search returns hundreds of records and none of them look right"}
You searched a sequence database instead of the Gene database. Searching
`BRCA1` in Nucleotide returns every deposited sequence anyone has ever
submitted that mentions it, which is thousands of records. Start at Gene, then
follow the link to the transcript.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The version suffix on the page is higher than the one printed here"}
The sequence has been corrected since this was written, which is the system
working. Use the current version and note it in your answer. This exercise is
about reading the record, not about matching this page.
:::

::: {.errfix err="Your coordinates do not match the ones in a paper you are reading"}
Check the assembly. If the paper is older than about 2015 it's probably GRCh37,
also called hg19. NCBI and Ensembl both have remapping tools, and neither will
guess for you.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The gene page shows several transcripts and you cannot tell them apart"}
Look for the MANE Select flag. If you're not working in human, there won't be
one, and the convention is to take the longest curated transcript with an `NM_`
prefix. Say which one you took.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Read an accession number and say what its prefix, its number, and its version
  suffix each mean
- Find the MANE Select transcript for a human gene, and say why there isn't one
  for mouse
- Explain why a single gene record can report three different exon counts
  without any of them being wrong
- Convert a coding-sequence range into a protein length and check it against
  the record
- Say what's missing from a genomic coordinate that has no assembly named
  alongside it
:::
